lesson.title: From Position to Velocity: Differentiating Motion
lesson.summary: If s(t) gives an object's position at time t, its velocity function v(t) = s'(t) is the derivative of position, telling you the object's exact rate of motion at every instant.
lesson.body:
Average velocity, change in position divided by change in time, tells you how an object did over some stretch of time, but it blurs together everything that happened in between. Instantaneous velocity, the velocity at one exact moment, is what you get by shrinking that time interval down to zero, which is precisely the definition of a derivative. So velocity is not a new idea bolted onto calculus; it's the instantaneous-velocity concept you've already learned, applied specifically to a position function.

If s(t) is position at time t, then velocity is v(t) = s'(t) = ds/dt. Since v(t) is itself a function of t, it can be differentiated again, and doing so is exactly how the next chapter defines acceleration, so velocity sits right in the middle of the differentiation chain that starts at position.

Suppose an object moves along a line so that its position in meters at time t seconds (for t greater than or equal to 0) is s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t. Differentiate to get velocity: v(t) = 3t^2 - 12t + 9, which factors as v(t) = 3(t - 1)(t - 3). Evaluating at a few times: v(0) = 9 m/s, v(1) = 3(0)(-2) = 0 m/s, v(2) = 3(1)(-1) = -3 m/s, v(3) = 3(2)(0) = 0 m/s, and v(4) = 3(3)(1) = 9 m/s.

These numbers already tell a story. The object starts out moving at 9 m/s, slows to a complete stop at t = 1 second, has negative velocity at t = 2 (meaning it's moving in the opposite direction), returns to rest at t = 3 seconds, and is back to 9 m/s by t = 4. This same position function will carry through the rest of this unit: acceleration, jerk, direction of motion, and speeding up versus slowing down all build directly on this one worked example, so it's worth keeping these numbers in mind.
